plainLanguageExplanation: Resistance is how much a material fights the flow of electric current — like friction slowing water in a rough pipe. It is measured in ohms (Ω). The more resistance, the harder the current has to push through, and with the same voltage you get less current: that's the famous pair, current = voltage ÷ resistance. Two things matter most: material (copper flows easily, rubber blocks almost entirely) and geometry (a long, thin path resists more than a short, thick one). In this model a resistor block sits on a metal rail; slide it to make the current travel a longer path and watch the ammeter sag and the bulb dim. Flip the material switch to copper and the same path suddenly pours current — tiny resistance. Resistance is the dimmer switch of the world: the filament of every bulb, the wire gauge in your walls, the resistor chips on circuit boards — all just drags the current is fighting against.

whyItMatters: Resistance is the control knob of electricity: it's why bulb filaments glow, why wires are sized by gauge, why fuses burn, and why resistors exist on boards. Design any circuit and you are really choosing resistances — too high and nothing flows, too low and wires melt. Understanding ohms is understanding why materials and shapes behave so differently in circuits.
didYouKnow: Copper conducts a billion billion times better than rubber. A single copper atom in a crystal lets its outer electrons flow almost freely — resistance is basically how crowded and bumpy the electron road is.
